title: The Eloquent Peasant

sources.author: W. M. Flinders Petrie
sources.title: Egyptian Tales, Translated from the Papyri, First Series

provenance.rights: The text is our own retelling of an ancient Egyptian tale, the Eloquent Peasant, written for Omramo; it does not use the wording of the cited edition. The cited edition is in the US public domain (published before 1931); other territories not verified. Legal review pending (PRD Q23).

geography.lesson: The peasant walks from the Salt Field, which most scholars place in the Wadi Natrun, a salt valley in the desert west of the Nile Delta, south to Herakleopolis, near today’s Beni Suef. His road runs from dry desert edge into the green, watered valley of the Nile.

culture.lesson: Ma’at, truth and balance, was the duty every Egyptian official claimed to keep. Scribes wrote on papyrus with reed pens, and pieces of copies of this tale made almost 4,000 years ago still survive.

moral.lesson: Khunanup wins because he will not stop speaking, but the powerful men who could have helped him at once keep silent on purpose, to enjoy his words. The child can weigh both sides of that silence.
moral.reflectionQuestion: Rensi and the king kept silent so that the peasant would keep talking. Was that fair to him, and what would you have done in Rensi’s place?

moral: Keep speaking up when you are wronged, for those with power must be fair.

cover.alt: A peasant in a short linen kilt stands with one hand raised, speaking, before a steward seated in a pale courtyard of lotus-bud columns, while a scribe writes on a papyrus roll and two grey donkeys wait by the gate.

tapTargets.title: The Salt Field
tapTargets.line: The peasant’s home country, a salt-crusted desert valley that most scholars place west of the Nile Delta.

cultureNote.label: From ancient Egypt
cultureNote.text: Most scholars place it in the Wadi Natrun, a valley named for its natron, though Petrie in 1895 put it beside the Fayum lake. Egyptians used natron, a natural salt, to clean, to make glazed faience and to dry and preserve the bodies of the dead.

tapTargets.pictureAlt: A shallow lake edged with a white crust of salt, with two date palms on the far bank.

tapTargets.title: Pack donkeys
tapTargets.line: Small, tough grey donkeys that carried loads for Egyptian farmers and traders on every road and path.

cultureNote.label: From ancient Egypt
cultureNote.text: Donkeys were tamed in north-east Africa more than 5,000 years ago, and for thousands of years they were Egypt’s carriers. Horses reached Egypt only after this story was written, and camels came into common use much later still.

tapTargets.pictureAlt: One small grey donkey with a dark stripe across its shoulders, carrying two bulging packs in rope nets.

tapTargets.title: Ma’at
tapTargets.line: The Egyptian word for truth, balance and fairness: the right order of the world that every judge must keep.

cultureNote.label: From ancient Egypt
cultureNote.text: The Egyptians pictured Ma’at as a goddess with an ostrich feather on her head, or as the feather alone. They believed a dead person’s heart was weighed against that feather. Officials boasted in their tombs that they had done ma’at.

tapTargets.pictureAlt: A single tall ostrich feather standing upright on one pan of a simple balance.

tapTargets.title: The scribe
tapTargets.line: A trained writer who kept records, letters and laws, writing with a reed pen on papyrus.

cultureNote.label: From ancient Egypt
cultureNote.text: A scribe’s palette held two cakes of ink: black for most words, red for headings and dates. Only a few Egyptians in every hundred could read and write, though nobody knows the number exactly, and boys trained for years to learn.

tapTargets.pictureAlt: A scribe’s long wooden palette with two round cakes of ink, one black and one red, and three reed pens.

framingDevice.label: LONG AFTER THIS STORY
framingDevice.line: Egyptians kept words safe on papyrus rolls for thousands of years. Long after this story, a great library of rolls grew in Alexandria, and today a new one stands near the same shore.

paras: ^At the edge of the western desert, in a valley of salt, there lived a man named <name:khunanup>Khunanup</name>.

His house was mud brick, flat-roofed, with two date palms leaning over it. Beyond them lay a shallow lake, and round its rim the ground had dried into a white crust that cracked under the foot like the top of a loaf. That crust was salt and natron, and it was why people called this place the <tap:salt-field>Salt Field</tap>.
Nothing grew there that a family could live on for long. So when the barley in the store jar ran low, Khunanup loaded his donkeys and went down into the valley of the Nile to trade.

He loaded them with everything the desert edge could give: sacks of salt and natron, bundles of reeds and rushes, pelts of desert animals, bags of seeds, live birds in cages, and straight staves of wood bound with cord.

> To his wife he said, <say:khunanup*>“Measure out the barley that is left. Keep enough for you and the children until I come back.”</say> She measured it into six small heaps on the floor. He looked at them for a long moment, then picked up his stick and whistled the donkeys awake.
For days the little <tap:donkey-caravan>string of donkeys</tap> picked its way south along the desert edge. The ground was stone and gravel, and the sun stood on their backs from morning until dusk.
Then, between one hill and the next, the world turned green. Below lay the valley: barley standing in square fields, canals as straight as ruled lines, and the river beyond, flat and shining.

Here the road shrank to a narrow raised path, with a canal on one side and a field of barley on the other. Beside the path stood a fine house with a garden wall. It belonged to a man called <name:nemtynakht>Nemtynakht</name>, who looked after these lands for a much greater man.
Nemtynakht was standing at his gate when the donkeys came by. He looked at their packs. He looked at the peasant, alone and far from home. And a thought came to him as smooth as oil.

> He called a servant. <say:nemtynakht*>“Bring me the longest length of linen we have,”</say> he said. <say:nemtynakht>“The good one.”</say> And when it came, he had it laid across the whole path, from the lip of the canal to the first stalks of his barley.
Khunanup came along the path with his donkeys and stopped. The cloth lay in front of him, fine linen, much too good for the dust.
<say:nemtynakht*>“Mind your feet, peasant,”</say> said Nemtynakht. <say:nemtynakht>“That linen is worth more than your whole load.”</say>

<say:khunanup*>“I meant no harm, sir,”</say> said Khunanup, and he turned his donkeys up the bank, where the footing was steep and crumbling. But up there the barley grew right to the edge. <say:nemtynakht*>“And now you would trample my grain?”</say> cried Nemtynakht.

<say:khunanup*>“Your cloth is on the road, and your barley is on the bank,”</say> said Khunanup. <say:khunanup>“Where would you have me walk? In the canal?”</say> As he spoke, the first donkey stretched out its neck and pulled up one mouthful of barley, ears and all.

> Nemtynakht smiled. <say:nemtynakht*>“Your donkey eats my barley. So your donkey is mine.”</say> He struck the peasant once with a tamarisk switch and drove all the donkeys through his gate. <say:nemtynakht>“Complain if you like. Who listens to a peasant?”</say>
For ten days Khunanup came back to that gate. He stood in the dust outside the garden wall and called through it, morning and evening.
<say:khunanup*>“Give me back my donkeys. One mouthful of barley, and you have taken everything I own. My children are waiting for grain.”</say>
Sometimes a servant laughed at him from the roof. Mostly nobody answered at all. Behind the wall, his donkeys brayed when they heard his voice, and that was the worst of it.

On the eleventh morning he asked a boatman whose land this was. The boatman pointed upstream with his chin. All of it, he said, belonged to the household of the High Steward, <name:rensi>Rensi son of Meru</name>, who sat in judgement for the king in the city of Herakleopolis.

> Khunanup had sold salt in village markets all his life. He had never spoken to anyone greater than a headman. He stood a while by the canal, turning the name over in his mouth like a pebble, and then he began to walk.

He found <name:rensi>Rensi</name> at the river landing, coming down the steps of his house to his boat. The boat had a painted cabin and two great steering oars, and a crowd of officials in long white kilts walked behind him, talking all at once.

Khunanup pushed to the front and told his story: the cloth, the barley, the single mouthful, the stick, the donkeys behind the wall. Rensi listened without a word. Then he turned to the men around him.

“Most likely he is some landowner’s peasant who has run off to a neighbour,” said one. “Is a man like Nemtynakht to be punished because a salt-seller says so? Let the donkeys go back, and that is the end of it.” The others nodded.
Rensi said nothing at all. He stood with one foot on the gangplank, looking at the peasant, and the officials began to shift and cough.

> Khunanup saw that silence and took it for the end. Something rose in him then that was not fear. He took one step closer, lifted his head, and spoke to the king’s High Steward as if they were the only two men on the bank.
^The first speech came out of him like water through a broken dyke.

<say:khunanup*>“My lord,”</say> he said, <say:khunanup>“you stand at the steering oar of this whole land. When you hold the oar true, the boat runs straight and every one of us aboard comes safe to the landing. But if the steersman leans, the whole boat leans with him.”</say>

<say:khunanup*>“In my village they say that when a child loses its father, or a woman is left alone, it is to your door they go, and they do not come away empty. I have walked a long way to learn whether that is true.”</say>

<say:khunanup*>“Do <tap:maat>ma’at</tap>, my lord: keep the world level, so the weak do not slide off it. My donkeys are all I have. Give them back, and I will tell every traveller on the salt road that the steward’s word is good.”</say>

> He stopped, out of breath. The officials had gone quiet. Rensi looked at him for a long time, and his face gave nothing away. Then he stepped down into his boat, and the oarsmen pushed off, and the peasant was left alone on the landing.
But Rensi did not go about his business that day. He had himself rowed to the palace, and he went in to the king, Nebkaura, with the peasant’s words still going round in his head.

<say:rensi*>“My lord,”</say> he said, <say:rensi>“there is a peasant at my landing who speaks better than any poet at your court. His donkeys were stolen, and he has come to me for justice. And every word he uses is the right one.”</say>

The king leaned forward and smiled. “Send bread to him each day, and grain to his house in the Salt Field, from a hand he cannot trace,” he said. “But keep your lips shut and let him run on. Put a scribe beside you, and bring me every word.”

> So the next morning, when Khunanup came back, a <tap:scribe>scribe</tap> was waiting in the steward’s courtyard. He sat cross-legged on a mat, a papyrus roll open across his knees and a reed pen behind his ear, and he did not look up.

Day after day Khunanup came to the courtyard, and day after day Rensi sat in his chair and said nothing. Each evening a man the peasant did not know pressed a loaf and a jug of beer into his hands at the gate. He thought it was some kindness of the city, and he ate it without asking.

The second time he spoke, his voice was harder. <say:khunanup*>“You are the scales, my lord. A scale does not lean toward the richer man. You are the plumb line hanging straight beside the wall. If you tip, who will set the world level again? A crooked balance cheats a whole market, and you are the balance for all Egypt.”</say>
The scribe’s pen scratched. Rensi’s face did not change. Khunanup stared at him and felt the anger climb up his throat.

> <say:khunanup*>“Do you hear me?”</say> he shouted. <say:khunanup>“I might as well plead with the river and beg it to run backwards!”</say> The pigeons on the roof went up all at once, and still the steward said nothing.
The days became weeks. The barley in the fields outside the city turned from green to gold, and still Khunanup came, and still the steward was silent.

He spoke a fourth time, and a fifth. He spoke on the steps of the temple, and at the landing as the boat came in. He spoke to Rensi’s back as the steward walked away. People in the market began to know his face. Some of them laughed. A few stopped to listen.

One morning the gatekeeper put his staff across the doorway. <say:khunanup*>“I have come to speak to the steward,”</say> said <name:khunanup>Khunanup</name>. “Not today,” said the gatekeeper. “Not any day. Go home, salt man.”
Khunanup sat down in the dust outside the gate. He thought of his wife counting out barley that must be gone by now. He thought of going home with nothing.

> Then he stood up, shook out his kilt, and waited. When the steward came out at noon, Khunanup was there in front of him, as he had been every day. <say:khunanup*>“My lord,”</say> he said, <say:khunanup>“I have not finished.”</say>
This was the ninth time he had stood before Rensi, and he knew it would be the last. He was tired now. His voice was quiet, and the scribe had to lean forward to catch it.

<say:khunanup*>“You speak well, my lord, when you speak at all. Your judges speak well. The whole city is full of fine words. But a fine word is not a just deed. A lovely sentence never filled an empty jar or brought a donkey home.”</say>

<say:khunanup*>“I have pleaded with you nine times, and nine times you have looked at me as if I were the wind. So I will stop pleading here. I will take my case to Anubis instead.”</say> It was a quiet thing to say, and a fearful one. The Egyptians believed that Anubis led the dead to their judgement, where each heart was weighed and no gift could tip the scales.

> Then he turned his back on the High Steward and walked out through the gate into the glare of noon. He had gone twenty paces down the street when he heard sandals slapping behind him. Two of Rensi’s guards were running to catch him.
^Khunanup thought they had come to punish him for his words.
He did not run. He let them take his arms and walk him back through the gate and into the courtyard, where <name:rensi>Rensi</name> had risen from his chair for the first time in all those days.

<say:rensi*>“Come, Khunanup. No one here will harm you,”</say> said the steward. It was the first time the peasant had heard his voice, and the first time anyone in that city had spoken his name. <say:rensi>“Sit down. There is something you must see.”</say>

The scribe came forward with his arms full. He knelt and began to unroll the <tap:library-moment>papyrus</tap> across the floor, sheet joined to sheet, and it kept on coming: column after column of small black marks, with here and there a line in red.

> <say:rensi*>“Your words,”</say> said Rensi. <say:rensi>“All of them. The first speech on the landing, and the one about the scales, and what you said today. Nine speeches, every one.”</say> The peasant looked down at the long pale road of writing and could not read a single mark of it.

Then Rensi told him the rest. The king had ordered the silence. The bread at the gate each evening had come from the steward’s own kitchens. And all this time, out in the Salt Field, his wife and children had been sent grain, though no one told them where it came from.

Khunanup did not know what to feel first. He had been fed like a guest and treated like a stone. For all those weeks he had believed no one was listening, and the whole time someone had been writing down every breath.

<say:khunanup*>“You let me beg,”</say> he said slowly, <say:khunanup>“so that the king could enjoy the begging.”</say> <say:rensi*>“I let you speak,”</say> said Rensi, <say:rensi>“so that the king could hear you. Now every word is written, and the king himself will read it.”</say>

> The rolls went to the palace that same afternoon. Later the servants said that the king read them through twice, that he laughed aloud at some lines and sat silent a long while over others. Then he sent word back to Rensi: “The case is yours to settle.”

<name:nemtynakht>Nemtynakht</name> was brought to the courtyard the next morning. He came in his best linen, with oil in his hair, and he smiled at the officials he knew. Then he saw the peasant standing beside the steward’s chair, and the smile went out of his face.
Rensi did not make a speech. He had heard enough speeches. He had the scribe read out the peasant’s first complaint from the landing, and then he gave his judgement in a few plain words.

<say:rensi*>“The donkeys go back to their owner, with every sack they carried. And because you took from a man who had almost nothing, Nemtynakht, all that you have goes to him: your house, your fields, your barley, your goods.”</say>
Nemtynakht opened his mouth. Then he looked at the long roll on the scribe’s knees, and shut it again.

> Khunanup found that he had nothing to say either. He, who had talked through nine long speeches, stood in the courtyard with his hands empty and his throat tight, and all he could do was bow low to the steward, and then, lower, to the scribe.
He went home by the river road when the heat began to ease, with his own donkeys in front of him and Nemtynakht’s behind. Every pack was heavy with grain, and the sacks swayed as the animals walked.

At the landing he stopped to look back once at the city: the pale walls, the steward’s boat at its post, the palms along the water. Somewhere behind those walls a scribe was already copying the nine speeches onto a fresh roll, his pen dipping and scratching, dipping and scratching.

Other scribes copied that roll, and others copied theirs, because people liked the story and wanted it for themselves. Parts of four of those copies, almost 4,000 years old, lie in museums today, and people still read them.

> But <name:khunanup>Khunanup</name> knew nothing of that. He was walking north, his stick on his shoulder, toward a mud-brick house by a lake of salt, where the six heaps of barley were long gone and a woman stood in the doorway, shading her eyes, counting donkeys.

landmarks.name: Bibliotheca Alexandrina

built.note: Building years of the new library, which opened in October 2002. The ancient Library of Alexandria it remembers was founded under the Ptolemies about 2,300 years ago and is lost.

low.line: A huge round building tilted toward the sea, its stone wall carved with letters from all over the world.

medium.line: A great modern library in Alexandria, Egypt, opened in 2002 near where the ancient library once stood.
medium.note: Egypt built it with help from many other countries, to a design by Snøhetta, a firm of architects from Norway. Its round roof tilts toward the sea like a rising sun.

advanced.line: The ancient Library of Alexandria was founded about 2,300 years ago and held many thousands of papyrus rolls.
advanced.note: No one knows for certain how it was lost. Old stories blame a single great fire, but most historians now think it faded slowly over centuries as money and care ran out. The new library has room for millions of books.

sourceNotes: This is our own retelling, written for Omramo, of the ancient Egyptian tale of the Eloquent Peasant.
It is not the wording of any earlier edition or translation.
Documented source: W. M. Flinders Petrie, "Egyptian Tales, Translated from the Papyri, First Series"
(1895), Project Gutenberg ebook #7386, https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/7386. In that book the tale is
titled "The Peasant and the Workman", under the heading "In the Sekhet Hemat, IXth Dynasty".
Source read: the mirror's 7386-0.txt gave 404; 7386.txt worked. The writer read it through a fetch tool
as a neutral summary (names, order of events, the papyri), for the order of events only. No sentence,
image or turn of phrase of Petrie's was used. A source-check agent must still compare the text with #7386.
Names: we use modern readings. Petrie -> ours: Sekhti -> Khunanup (Khun-Anup); Hemti son of Asri ->
Nemtynakht (son of Isri; older books also read Djehutinakht); Meruitensa -> Rensi son of Meru;
Neb-ka-n-ra -> Nebkaura (Nebkaure Khety, a Herakleopolitan king); Sekhet Hemat ('salt country') ->
the Salt Field, thought to be the Wadi Natrun; Henenseten (Petrie identifies it as Herakleopolis,
modern Ihnasya / Ahnas) -> Herakleopolis. Egyptologist to confirm every reading.
Departures from Petrie, following later translations of the fuller papyri (reviewer to confirm):
barley, not Petrie's 'corn'; TEN days of pleading with Nemtynakht (Petrie: a whole day); the ninth
petition's appeal to Anubis (not in Petrie's text as read). The wife's barley and the goods list
are given loosely; the six heaps of barley follow the later translations' six measures (to check).
Nine petitions become three spoken speeches (first, the scales, the last) plus a short account of the
rest. The speeches' images (steersman, orphan and widow, scales and plumb line, fine words versus just
deeds) follow the tale's themes in our own words; none is a translation of a petition.
Softened / left out: the beating with tamarisk is one strike; the beating by Rensi's men at the third
petition is left out (a gatekeeper turns him away instead); the 'Demon of Silence' threat is left out;
the officials' advice to bring a witness is folded into their dismissal. The exact rations (Petrie:
four loaves and two jugs of beer a day; corn for the wife) are given as a loaf and a jug of beer.
Ending: the source's end is damaged. We keep its judgement (the donkeys back and Nemtynakht's goods and
house to the peasant) and leave out the offices and the peasant becoming the king's favourite.
Our own additions: the boatman, the gatekeeper, the market crowd, the king reading twice ('the servants
said'), the scene of Nemtynakht's silence, the cool-season walk home, the wife counting donkeys.
Card and text facts to check: Wadi Natrun named for natron and identified with the Salt Field; uses of
natron; donkeys tamed in NE Africa over 5,000 years ago; horses in Egypt after this tale, camels much
later; Ma'at's feather and the weighing of the heart; literacy 'a few in every hundred' (estimates vary);
'parts of four copies survive' (Berlin P3023, P3025, P10499 and the Butler papyrus, plus Amherst
fragments; Petrie names three plus fragments); 'almost 4,000 years old' (late Middle Kingdom copies).
Landmark facts to check: Bibliotheca Alexandrina built 1995-2002, opened Oct 2002, by Snohetta with
international support; granite wall carved with signs of many scripts; room for millions of books;
ancient library founded under the Ptolemies about 2,300 years ago; its loss gradual and uncertain.
Open question for the editor: the 'jug of beer' is true to the source and to Egyptian diet; keep or
change for the young end of the audience? And is the Anubis line right at this level?
SOURCE CHECK (18 Nov 2026, against Petrie on the Gutenberg mirror):
Echoes reworded: the king's last word ('Judge it yourself' -> 'The case is yours to settle'); the
king's orders (were clause by clause; now reordered and compressed: bread, silence, scribe); the cloth
(no 'fringe'; now 'the longest length of linen'); 'tread on my clothes' (now the linen's worth);
the orphan's-father / widow's-husband image (now: the bereaved go to his door); 'a few sacks of salt'
(now 'because a salt-seller says so'); 'Do not be afraid' (now 'No one here will harm you').
Departures from Petrie: in Petrie the peasant already knows the land is the steward's and says so
before the beating; ours learns it later from a boatman. In Petrie he first sends his account through
one of the steward's followers, who puts it to the nobles; ours tells Rensi directly. Rensi's oath that
the peasant shall be remembered for ever is left out.
Factual: Petrie places the Sekhet Hemat at the edge of the Fayum lake, not the Wadi Natrun. The Wadi
Natrun identification is that of later scholars; the salt-field card and geography lesson now say
'most scholars place it' and the card names Petrie's view. region.place keeps the plan's wording.

palette.mood: Salt white and sand gold under wide pale skies; the green of barley and the slow blue of the Nile in the lower third; one cool note of blue lotus. Bright, dry, still air. Calm, sunlit and grown-up, like a tomb painting seen through morning haze.

artBrief.light: This is a LIGHT story: every scene has a pale sky or pale wall behind the words on both panes. Early morning white-gold at the Salt Field and on the path; soft cream daylight in the courtyard, with short shadows under the columns; pale rose-gold late afternoon at the river. No night, no deep shadow behind text. The dark ink #1C2433 must read on every pane.
world: Egypt about 4,000 years ago (the tale is set under a king of Herakleopolis, about 2100 BCE, and was written down in the Middle Kingdom, about 1850 BCE). Middle Kingdom look throughout.

The Salt Field (Wadi Natrun): a low desert valley with shallow lakes whose edges dry to a white, slightly pinkish crust of salt and natron; reeds at the water, a few date palms, gravel desert rising beyond.

Houses: mud brick, flat roofs (sometimes a light shelter of reeds on the roof), small high windows, plastered and whitewashed; a store jar of clay by the door. Rich houses have a garden wall and palms.
The valley: barley and emmer wheat in square fields, flax with small blue flowers, straight canals with raised earth paths along them; sycamore figs, acacia and tamarisk; date and dom palms.

Men: peasants in a short white linen kilt or loincloth, bare-chested, barefoot or in reed sandals, short dark hair. Officials in a longer kilt to the shin, a broad collar of beads (blue, green, red), sometimes a short wig, a long staff of office.
Women: a plain white sheath dress with shoulder straps, long dark hair; children often go without clothes in the heat, but draw them in short kilts or simple shifts for this app.
Donkeys: small, grey, with a dark stripe over the shoulders and long ears; loads in rope nets or bags slung on both sides. They are the only pack animals in this story.

Rensi's courtyard: pale plastered walls, columns shaped like bundles of papyrus stems or with closed lotus-bud tops, painted in soft red, blue and green bands; reed mats; Rensi's chair has carved lion legs.

The scribe: sits cross-legged with his kilt pulled tight to make a desk; a long wooden palette with two cakes of ink (black and red), reed pens, a water pot; the papyrus roll is pale yellow-cream. Writing is shown only as rows or columns of small dark marks with a few red lines, never readable or invented signs.

Boats: a wooden Nile boat with a curved hull, a cabin of painted wood or reed matting amidships, one or two big steering oars at the stern, oarsmen; a tall mast with a tall narrow sail may be lowered at the landing.
Food: round flat loaves and pottery beer jugs with clay stoppers; sacks of grain of coarse linen.
Nothing frightening or cruel: the single stick-strike on page 3 is not shown; Anubis is never drawn.

Avoid: pyramids, the Sphinx and any pyramid-and-palm skyline; camels; horses, chariots and carts (horses came about 1650 BCE); the shaduf water-lift (later, New Kingdom); Tutankhamun gold, the striped nemes headdress, Cleopatra kohl glamour, Arab or Ottoman dress, minarets; mummies; readable hieroglyphs.

characters.khunanup: A man of about thirty, about three heads tall, wiry and sun-browned, with short dark hair and small plain eyes; clean-shaven. A short white linen kilt grown grey with dust, reed sandals, a cord belt with a small linen pouch. Signature detail: his long walking stick, and later his one raised hand when he speaks. Expression through posture: stooped and dusty in Part I, upright in Part II, very still in Part III.
characters.rensi: A calm, heavy-set man in his fifties, about three heads tall, with a short black wig and small plain eyes. A long white kilt to the shin with a finer see-through over-kilt, and a broad collar of blue, green and red beads. Signature detail: the long staff of office and his hands folded on it; he sits very still. Grand but never cruel.
characters.nemtynakht: A well-fed, neat man in fine white linen to the knee, oiled hair, a small bead collar, holding a thin green tamarisk switch. Smug, not monstrous: no snarling face. In Part III the same man, stiff and silent.

scene-oasis.unfolded: Early morning, white-gold. The upper 60 percent of both panes is pale sky fading to cream at the horizon. Far: the low gravel desert. Middle: the shallow lake with its white salt crust and a few date palms. Near, low on the right half: the flat-roofed mud-brick house, Khunanup tying loads on three or four grey donkeys, his wife and two children at the doorway. On the left, low, a strip of salt crust and reeds only.
scene-oasis.folded: Khunanup tying a rope net of salt onto a grey donkey, low in the frame, his wife at the door behind; pale sky above for the words.

scene-path.unfolded: Morning, pale gold sky over the upper 60 percent. Low across both panes: a straight canal on the left side of the path and a green barley field on the right. On the right half: Nemtynakht's whitewashed house behind a garden wall and palms, the fringed linen cloth laid across the whole path, Nemtynakht beside it with a thin switch, and the donkeys halted in a line with Khunanup at the front.
scene-path.folded: Nemtynakht with his switch beside the cloth on the path, the first grey donkey stopped at its edge; pale sky above.

scene-hall.unfolded: Soft cream daylight. The upper 60 percent is pale plastered wall and sky above a low roof line, with the tops of two lotus-bud columns. Low on the right: Rensi on his lion-legged chair, a scribe cross-legged on a mat with a papyrus roll, and Khunanup standing with one hand raised. Officials stand to one side. On the last pages a long papyrus roll lies unrolled across the floor.
scene-hall.folded: Khunanup standing, one hand raised, beside the seated scribe writing on a papyrus roll; pale wall above.

scene-river.unfolded: Late afternoon, pale rose-gold sky over the upper 60 percent. The Nile wide and calm across the lower third, green fields and palms on the far bank, desert cliffs faint beyond. On the right half: stone steps down to the landing and Rensi's boat with its painted cabin and steering oars, a few officials. Small on a path past the fields, a man leading loaded donkeys away (serves the last page).
scene-river.folded: Rensi's boat at the landing with its cabin and steering oars, officials on the steps; pale sky above.

pictures.salt-field: A shallow lake with a white crust of salt along its edge and two date palms on the far bank, centred under a pale sky.
pictures.donkey-caravan: One small grey donkey with a dark shoulder stripe and two bulging packs in rope nets, standing side-on, centred.
pictures.maat: A single tall ostrich feather standing upright on one pan of a simple wooden balance, centred on a deep blue ground.
pictures.scribe: A scribe's long wooden palette with two round cakes of ink, black and red, and three reed pens, lying flat and centred.

portraits.khunanup: Half figure in his dusty short kilt, one hand raised mid-speech, walking stick in the other hand, pale sky and salt lake behind.
portraits.rensi: Half figure seated, hands folded on his staff, broad bead collar, calm closed face, pale courtyard columns behind.

artBrief.cover: Rensi's courtyard in soft daylight: Khunanup standing with one hand raised, speaking; Rensi silent on his lion-legged chair; a scribe cross-legged writing on a long papyrus roll that spills across the floor; two grey donkeys waiting by the gate.

landmarks.bibliotheca-alexandrina: Our own drawing of the library as it is today, in clear daylight: the huge round tilted roof of glass and metal panels rising toward the sea, the curved grey granite wall carved with letters and signs of many scripts, a reflecting pool in front, the Mediterranean beyond. Architecture only; no photograph traced; no readable invented letters.
